control.topic: A customer asks Fox & Flour to create a celebration cake for an event tied to the neighborhood baking competition.
control.first_pass_raw: {"turns":[{"line_index":0,"speaker_alias":"ruby","text":"We just got a request for a celebration cake for an event connected to the neighborhood baking competition. I love that they thought of us for it, but I want to make sure we ask the right questions before I start picturing the whole thing."},{"line_index":1,"speaker_alias":"tyson","text":"Start with the practical ones: when is the event, how many people are they serving, and when do they need to pick it up? turns.text: We just got a celebration-cake request for the neighborhood baking competition event. I love that they thought of us.
Good. Did they say whether the cake is for the competitors, the crowd, or somebody who expects to win?

Then before we fall in love with an idea, we need the useful answers: when they need it, how many people it’s for, and what the occasion actually is.
You do know how to take the sparkle out of a sentence.
I take the panic out of pickup. Different service.
Fair. But “the neighborhood” gives us a lovely place to start. I’ve still been hoping Fox & Flour could have a welcoming mascot.
A mascot on a competition cake could be fun. It could also become twelve tiny details that no one can see once the candles are lit.
Not twelve tiny details. One clear, friendly one. The cake should feel celebratory, not like it entered the competition itself.
That’s the right line. We’ll ask for the event details first, then make the celebration cake the part people remember after the judging is over.
Perfect. And if the answer is “a fox,” I’m going to try very hard to act surprised.

treatment.topic: Ruby takes a call for a celebration cake tied to the neighborhood baking competition, only for Tyson to realize the customer's request could put Fox & Flour in an awkward position with the competing bakers.

A cake that arrives smiling and immediately starts a fight."},{"line_index":2,"speaker_alias":"ruby","text":"They said it was meant to be funny. They also want every competing baker’s name around the edge, so nobody feels left out. Except, apparently, everybody will feel left out."},{"line_index":3,"speaker_alias":"tyson","text":"If it’s sitting anywhere near the competition, that stops being a joke between friends. The awkward part isn’t the cake. turns.text: I just took a call about a celebration cake tied to the neighborhood baking competition. Sweet idea—until the last part.
That pause means it was not, in fact, a sweet idea.
They want us to make the cake, then they’ll put it on their own competition table as though they baked it.
Ah. That’s not a cake order. That’s somebody asking us to quietly become their entry.
They said it would only be “a little help.” I told them I’d check before promising anything.
Good. The other bakers are showing up with what they made. If Fox & Flour is sitting in one person’s display, that gets awkward fast.
I hate disappointing someone who called excited about a celebration.
Then don’t make it about disappointment. Tell them we can make a custom celebration cake for after the competition—when it can actually celebrate somebody.
That’s fair. We’re happy to make the cake, just not something passed off as their baking.
Exactly. A pickup should not require a secret identity.
I’m calling them back. And if they win honestly, I’ll be delighted to make the biggest celebration cake they can carry.
